**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Proposed response to rising inference demand

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing fleet before committing to any hardware purchase, while placing a small, cancellable order for one additional node as insurance. This is not a compromise for its own sake; it reflects our belief that the cheapest capacity we can get is capacity we already own, and that the decision to buy more is only well-informed once we know how much of our current hardware is genuinely idle versus genuinely saturated.

**Where we stand**

Our eight-node cluster currently runs at roughly 40 percent average GPU utilisation, but that average hides the real story. Peak-hour demand on our primary inference service pushes the four newest nodes close to saturation, while the four older nodes sit mostly idle outside of batch jobs. Latency at peak has crept from 180ms to a p95 of over 400ms, which is now visible in user-facing metrics and, we suspect, in retention. Meanwhile, our batch workloads queue for hours because they compete with interactive traffic for the same machines.

The obvious reading is that we need more of the new nodes. The more careful reading is that we have a scheduling and routing problem wearing the costume of a capacity problem. Right now, traffic lands wherever the load balancer happens to send it, with no awareness of model residency or node capability. A request that could run comfortably on an older node is just as likely to land on a saturated one, adding queue time for everyone. Fixing that is software work measured in engineer-weeks, not procurement measured in months.

**Cost**

A new node costs approximately £85k upfront plus meaningful power, cooling, and colocation costs, and given current supply chains, delivery is quoted at 10–14 weeks. The utilisation work, by contrast, is roughly six engineer-weeks of existing staff time. Even if the software work only lifts effective utilisation from 40 to 60 percent, that is equivalent to adding three nodes' worth of capacity for a fraction of the cost. There is also a hidden cost to buying now: we would be purchasing against a demand curve we have not yet validated. Our traffic spike may be a product launch echo rather than a durable trend, and capital spent on hardware that sits underused in six months is capital we cannot spend on hiring or on the model work that actually differentiates us.

**Latency**

The utilisation path helps latency in two ways. Better routing alone should cut p95 meaningfully by keeping interactive traffic off congested nodes. Separating batch and interactive workloads onto different pools removes the contention that causes our worst tail latencies. Buying hardware also helps latency, of course, but only after the 10–14 week delivery window, during which our p95 will likely keep degrading. The software path starts paying back within weeks.

**Reliability**

Here the purchase case is stronger, and we want to be honest about it. Eight nodes means that a single failure removes 12.5 percent of capacity, and our two oldest nodes are now three years into a five-year useful life with no redundancy behind them. If one dies, we feel it immediately. A ninth node would give us genuine headroom. This is why we recommend the small insurance order: one node, placed as a cancellable order, covers the reliability gap without committing us to the full expansion. It is the part of the buy-more argument that utilisation work cannot substitute for.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The asymmetry of reversibility matters more than any single number. Software improvements are cheap to reverse or redirect; if the routing work disappoints, we have lost weeks and learned exactly where the ceiling is. Hardware is sticky: once purchased, it carries depreciation, power, and maintenance obligations regardless of whether demand materialises, and reselling specialised accelerators is slow and loss-making. Buying first also forecloses the option of waiting for the next hardware generation, which vendors have signalled is roughly two quarters out with meaningful performance-per-watt gains.

**Uncertainty**

We are genuinely uncertain about two things. First, whether demand growth is durable; we have three months of data and a launch confound. Second, how far utilisation can realistically be pushed — 60 percent is an estimate, not a measurement, and some of the idle time may be structurally unavoidable. Both uncertainties resolve within a quarter, which is exactly why we should not spend irreversibly before they do.

**Proposed next steps**

We propose: begin the routing and workload-separation work immediately; place one cancellable node order as reliability insurance; re-evaluate the full purchase decision in twelve weeks with real utilisation data in hand. If demand holds and the software work stalls, we will have lost little. If it does not, we will have saved ourselves a very expensive mistake.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Local AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Status and the question in front of us**

Our four A100 nodes are running at roughly 62 percent average utilisation, but that number hides the real problem: peak demand regularly saturates the cluster, while nights and weekends sit nearly idle. Two teams have queued experiments they cannot run, and the inference service serving our internal search product is now bumping against latency SLOs during business hours. The proposal on the table is to purchase two additional nodes at approximately $310k all-in, including networking and rack integration. The alternative is to invest roughly six weeks of platform engineering time in scheduling, batching, and workload-shaping improvements to raise effective utilisation before spending anything.

**The cost picture, honestly stated**

The purchase price is only the visible part of the acquisition. Depreciation over a three-to-four-year useful life, power and cooling, and the operational burden of managing more hardware all compound. More importantly, GPU prices are on a downward trajectory as the next generation ships, and our workloads are still evolving — we do not yet know which of our fine-tuning efforts will survive contact with production. Buying now locks in today's prices for capacity whose ideal shape we cannot yet specify. By contrast, the utilisation work is paid for in engineer time we mostly already have, and its value compounds: every percentage point of utilisation we gain is capacity we never have to buy, power, or depreciate.

**Latency cuts both ways**

The strongest argument for buying is latency. Batch scheduling and queueing improvements help throughput workloads, but interactive inference latency is partly a physics problem — if the serving fleet is contended, no scheduler fixes tail latency. Our search product's p99 has degraded from 180ms to 340ms during peak hours, and that is a user-visible regression. However, much of that contention comes from batch jobs scheduled naively alongside serving traffic. If we enforce strict partitioning of serving capacity and move batch work into off-peak windows, we recover most of the latency headroom without new silicon. The risk is that partitioning reduces the flexibility that made the cluster useful in the first place; we should treat that as a tradeoff to measure, not assume.

**Reliability and the fragility of a bigger footprint**

Adding nodes does not obviously improve reliability. Our failure mode today is a single top-of-rack switch and a homogenous driver stack; doubling the fleet doubles the surface we must patch, monitor, and keep consistent, and our on-call rotation is already thin. Utilisation work, done well, actually improves reliability: proper queueing with backpressure prevents the silent contention that currently causes our worst incidents, and off-peak batch windows give us clean maintenance windows we lack today. The counterargument is real, though — if a utilisation-focused strategy pushes the cluster to 85–90 percent, we lose the slack that absorbs failures gracefully. Running hot is its own reliability risk, and we should not plan to operate above roughly 80 percent sustained.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The six engineer-weeks for scheduling and partitioning work are weeks not spent on product features, and that is a genuine cost. But it is small, bounded, and — critically — reversible. If the utilisation work stalls or the gains disappoint, we can still buy the nodes, having lost little except time. The purchase is the opposite: largely irreversible. Reselling GPUs recovers perhaps half the outlay, and the engineering effort to integrate then decommission hardware is pure waste. When one option is cheap, reversible, and informative, and the other is expensive and binding, the sequencing is not a close call. The utilisation work also generates data — real demand curves, real contention patterns — that will make any eventual purchase better targeted, or reveal it to be unnecessary.

**Recommendation**

Do not buy the nodes now. Fund a focused, six-week effort to partition serving from batch traffic, move bulk workloads off-peak, and add queueing with backpressure, targeting 80 percent sustained utilisation and restored p99 latency. Revisit the purchase decision at the end of that window with measured numbers in hand. If serving latency remains the binding constraint after partitioning — which I estimate at perhaps a one-in-three chance — buy then, with better information and likely better prices.

**Uncertainty**

Our utilisation telemetry is coarse, and self-reported demand from queued teams tends to overstate real need. Both the cost of the utilisation work and its gains could be off by a factor of two in either direction. That uncertainty is precisely why the reversible path comes first.

We should decide by end of month so the platform team can start before the quarterly planning freeze.

**MEMO: Local AI Capacity — Buy More Hardware or Improve Utilisation?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on our local inference capacity strategy

Over the past quarter, our local AI hardware has become the binding constraint on several projects. GPU queues have lengthened, batch jobs are being scheduled around peak interactive hours, and at least two teams have quietly started renting cloud capacity to fill gaps. The question in front of us is whether to purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out the trade-offs as I see them and make a recommendation, with the caveat that some of the numbers below are estimates and I'll flag where my confidence is low.

Let me start with cost, because it's the easiest to quantify and the most commonly over-weighted. A new high-end GPU node costs roughly the equivalent of two full-time engineers for a year once you include the machine itself, power, cooling, and the operational overhead of racking and maintaining it. Our utilisation analysis suggests our current fleet sits at around 35–40% average utilisation, with sharp peaks during working hours and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. If we could lift that to 60%, we would effectively add half a fleet's worth of capacity without buying anything. The engineering work involved — better job scheduling, a shared queue, model pooling, and some discipline around who can reserve what — is perhaps three to four engineer-months. On pure cost grounds, utilisation wins by a wide margin.

Latency complicates the picture. Much of our idle capacity is idle because interactive workloads demand headroom: when someone is iterating on a model or running a latency-sensitive service, we keep buffers free so response times stay predictable. Squeezing utilisation through aggressive packing tends to increase contention, and contention shows up as tail latency. For our batch and training workloads this is irrelevant; for the developer experience and the customer-facing inference we run locally, it matters a great deal. This is the strongest argument for buying hardware — headroom is cheap insurance against latency spikes, and no amount of clever scheduling fully substitutes for it.

Reliability cuts in a more interesting direction. Right now, losing our largest node takes out a meaningful fraction of total capacity, and we have felt this during two outages this year. A second argument for buying more hardware is that it diversifies our failure modes. But there's a counterpoint: better utilisation, if implemented as a proper scheduler with checkpointing and preemption, actually improves reliability under load, because jobs become movable rather than pinned to specific machines. Utilisation work, done well, is partly resilience work. Done badly — as ad hoc sharing with no queueing discipline — it makes outages worse. That risk is real and I don't want to minimise it.

Opportunity cost is where I think the decision actually turns. The engineers best placed to do the utilisation work are also our most senior infrastructure people, and their time is currently going into a project with direct revenue impact. Spending three to four of their months on internal tooling is not free; it delays that project. Conversely, buying hardware consumes capital but almost no engineering time — procurement, once approved, is mostly waiting. If our senior engineers' time is the scarcest resource, hardware is the cheaper option in the currency that matters. However, I'd note that the utilisation work could plausibly be done by a mid-level engineer with a senior person advising, which changes the calculus considerably.

Finally, reversibility. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible: capital spent is spent, and if our workload mix shifts — say, if we move more inference to a hosted provider for cost or compliance reasons — we own depreciating machines we can't easily sell. Utilisation improvements are software and process; they can be adjusted, extended, or abandoned cheaply, and the scheduling infrastructure we'd build is useful regardless of future hardware decisions. In an environment where our AI usage patterns have changed twice in the past year, I weight reversibility heavily.

**Recommendation:** Improve utilisation first, and defer the hardware purchase by two quarters. Concretely, that means standing up a shared scheduler with preemption, moving batch work into overnight windows, and setting an explicit utilisation target of 55–60% by end of next quarter. If we hit that target and queues are still painful, the case for hardware becomes straightforward and we will have better data on what to buy. If we miss it, we'll know the constraint is real rather than organisational.

**Uncertainty:** My utilisation figures come from coarse monitoring and could be off by several points; the engineering effort estimate is a guess from the people who'd do the work and has historically been optimistic. The largest risk is that we under-invest in the utilisation project, half-finish it, and end up buying hardware anyway having lost a quarter.

Reselling used accelerators is possible but typically at a steep discount.

The utilisation path looks different. Right now our fleet averages somewhere in the low-40s percent utilisation, with sharp peaks and deep valleys. That gap between average and peak is where the opportunity is. Better batching, request coalescing, model quantisation where quality permits, and smarter scheduling across our serving tiers could plausibly lift effective capacity by 30 to 50 percent without buying a single card. The cost here is engineering time — realistically a couple of engineers for a quarter — and that's the real opportunity cost of this option: those are people who won't be shipping features during that window. But unlike a hardware purchase, this investment is highly reversible and compounding. The scheduling and batching work we build now keeps paying off as we grow, and if it turns out we still need more capacity afterward, we'll be buying hardware knowing we'll run it hard rather than at half-throttle. There's also a reliability dividend: better headroom management and load shedding give us more graceful degradation under stress, which addresses the incident risk more precisely than raw capacity does.

On latency specifically, I want to be careful. Some of our p95 tail is genuinely a capacity problem, but some of it is scheduling and batching behaviour that more hardware would simply mask. If we buy first and optimise later, we'll likely discover we over-provisioned. If we optimise first, we get a much clearer signal about what we actually need.

So my recommendation is to pursue utilisation improvements first, with a defined scope and a decision point. Concretely: commit a small team to the batching, scheduling, and quantisation work over the next quarter, with a target of raising fleet utilisation into the low-60s and bringing p95 back inside our SLO. If we hit that target, we defer the purchase and revisit in two quarters with better data. If we fall materially short — or if demand growth outruns the gains — we proceed with the hardware purchase from a position of knowledge rather than guesswork, and the optimisation work will have made the new hardware cheaper to run well.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Utilisation gains of the size I'm describing are plausible but not guaranteed; some of it depends on workload characteristics we haven't fully profiled, and quantisation trade-offs need careful quality evaluation before we lean on them. There's also a risk that the optimisation effort becomes a distraction if it drags on — which is why I'd time-box it and define the exit criteria up front. And if our growth forecast is materially wrong on the upside, no amount of efficiency work will save us from needing to buy; the recommendation should be read as sequencing, not as a permanent alternative to capacity.

My overall judgment is that the reversible, information-rich option should come first. Buying hardware now solves the symptom quickly but at high cost and with low flexibility; improving utilisation solves much of the problem at lower cost, preserves our option to buy later with better information, and builds capability that compounds. Let's fund the optimisation work now and put a hardware decision on the calendar for the end of the quarter.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data and the cost model in detail at Thursday's review.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Internal circulation only

Over the past quarter we've hit the wall on our local inference hardware often enough that the question of capacity has moved from background grumbling to a real decision point. The instinctive response — buy more GPUs — is understandable, but I want to argue that it's premature, and that the better first move is a sustained effort to improve utilisation of the fleet we already own. The reasoning is as much about economics and optionality as it is about engineering.

Start with cost. Our current hardware is largely paid for; the marginal cost of squeezing another ten or fifteen percent of throughput out of it is essentially the engineering time we'd spend on batching, scheduling, quantisation, and smarter request routing. Buying new accelerators, by contrast, is a capital commitment that lands all at once, depreciates quickly in a market where model architectures and hardware generations turn over every eighteen months or so, and drags along hidden costs we tend to underestimate: power, cooling, rack space, and the operational burden of a more heterogeneous fleet. If we can defer that purchase by even two quarters while we fix utilisation, we buy time for hardware prices and capabilities to move — and they have been moving in our favour.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and it deserves honest treatment. Right now, our p95 latency degrades noticeably during peak windows because jobs queue behind each other and batch sizes balloon. More hardware would trivially fix this. But it's worth asking whether the latency we're protecting is actually the latency our users experience, or an artefact of how we've scheduled work. A significant share of our peak load is batch inference and fine-tuning runs that have no real-time deadline; they're on the same queues as interactive traffic because it was convenient, not because it was correct. Separating those workloads, pre-empting batch jobs when interactive traffic arrives, and right-sizing our batching windows should recover most of the peak-hour headroom we're missing — without a single new card.

Reliability cuts both ways. A larger fleet gives us more redundancy, and our current single-cluster setup does make us nervous: one hot-swappable node failure during a training run costs us hours. But adding hardware to a fleet we don't fully understand doesn't improve reliability so much as it adds more components that can fail in ways we haven't seen. Better utilisation work — proper health checks, checkpointing discipline, graceful drain-and-replace procedures — improves reliability on the fleet we have, and those practices transfer to whatever we buy later. Reliability is mostly a software and process property; we should not try to purchase our way out of a process gap.

The opportunity cost question is the one I keep returning to. The engineers who would integrate and operate new hardware are the same ones who would build the scheduling and serving improvements. If we spend the next quarter racking and configuring new boxes, we will not have built the serving layer that makes any fleet — current or future — actually efficient. Conversely, if we do the utilisation work first and it turns out we genuinely still need capacity, we'll know exactly how much, of what, and where the bottlenecks really are. That knowledge is worth more than the hardware itself, because it converts a guess into a specification.

Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale; it's a sunk cost the moment the purchase order clears, and reselling used accelerators recovers a fraction of the price. Improving utilisation is almost entirely reversible — we can stop, change approach, or accelerate it as evidence accumulates. When two options are plausibly similar in benefit, the reversible one is almost always the right first step, because it keeps the expensive, irreversible option available for when we actually need it.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next quarter to a focused utilisation programme — workload separation, dynamic batching, quantisation where quality permits, and proper queueing — with an explicit, pre-agreed trigger for revisiting the purchase decision. If, after that work, our p95 latency still breaches agreed thresholds during peak hours, or our projected growth implies saturation within two quarters, we buy, and we buy with confidence rather than anxiety.

I want to be clear about the uncertainty here. Utilisation improvements have a habit of delivering half of what their advocates promise, and it's possible our peak demand is simply real and growing faster than optimisation can absorb. If the team believes the numbers say otherwise, I'd rather hear that now than after a quarter of effort. But the evidence we have — idle overnight capacity, batch jobs blocking interactive traffic, and utilisation metrics that vary threefold across nodes — suggests there is real headroom. Let's use it before we buy more.

Comments welcome by

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Hardware purchase vs. utilisation improvement for our local inference capacity
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

We've reached the point where our local GPU fleet is running hot. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, a couple of recent service degradations were traced to saturation rather than software faults, and the natural instinct is to buy our way out. Before we commit, I want to argue that we should spend the next quarter improving utilisation of what we already own, with a purchase decision deferred until we have evidence that efficiency work alone cannot close the gap.

Start with cost. A new node of the class we've been quoting is roughly a quarter of a million dollars once you include networking, rack power, and the cooling headroom it will need. That figure is not catastrophic for our budget, but it is large enough that we should be confident we need it. Right now we are not. Our telemetry suggests average GPU utilisation across the fleet sits somewhere in the low forties, while peak utilisation on the busiest nodes exceeds ninety percent. That pattern is the classic signature of a scheduling and batching problem, not a capacity problem. We are paying for capacity we own and failing to use it where and when it matters. Buying more hardware before fixing that would mean paying twice for the same capability: once in capital and once in the ongoing power and maintenance of machines that sit idle most of the day.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to treat it fairly. The user-facing services that suffer most are the interactive ones, and for those, tail latency is the product. If a batch job hogs a GPU for ninety seconds, no amount of clever scheduling fully hides that from a user waiting on a response. But this is precisely the kind of problem that workload isolation, priority queues, and better batching windows are designed to solve, and we have barely attempted them. Our current scheduler was built when we had three machines and one workload. It has not been seriously revisited since. There is meaningful headroom there, and the industry experience with inference serving stacks suggests that well-tuned batching and disaggregated prefill can cut tail latencies substantially on identical hardware.

Reliability cuts both ways. More nodes means more redundancy, and our single-node failure domains are genuinely uncomfortable; when the node hosting the embeddings service went down last month, we had no local fallback. But redundancy bought through underutilised hardware is the most expensive kind. If we consolidate workloads intelligently, we can free up specific machines to act as warm spares, giving us the same failure tolerance at zero incremental capital cost. Conversely, if we buy now, we will likely spread workloads across the enlarged fleet in the same haphazard way, and our reliability will remain a function of luck rather than design.

The opportunity cost deserves honest weight. Every dollar and, more importantly, every engineer-month spent on procurement, installation, and integration is a dollar and a month not spent on the product features that actually differentiate us. Efficiency work is not free either, and I don't want to pretend it is; scheduler rewrites have a way of expanding in scope. But the efficiency work is largely a one-time investment that compounds, whereas the purchase is a recurring commitment in power, maintenance, and eventually depreciation. There is also a real risk that we buy hardware and then, six months later, a model architecture change or a quantisation breakthrough makes that class of accelerator obsolete or unnecessary. That risk argues for waiting.

Which brings me to reversibility, the consideration I trust most. Buying hardware is nearly irreversible at our scale. Reselling used accelerators recovers a fraction of cost, and the lead time to procure means the decision locks us in for years. Improving utilisation is almost perfectly reversible: if our scheduler changes fail, we revert; if they succeed, we've delayed or shrunk a purchase. When one option is reversible and the other is not, and both plausibly address the problem, the reversible option should be tried first unless the cost of being wrong is catastrophic. I don't believe it is. Our worst case is another quarter of degraded peak-hour latency, which is painful but survivable.

So my recommendation is concrete: we commit two engineers to a focused utilisation effort this quarter, targeting workload consolidation, priority scheduling, and a warm-spare reliability posture, with explicit success criteria around p99 latency and fleet utilisation. We revisit the purchase decision at the end of that quarter with real data in hand. If the numbers still say we need capacity, we will buy with far better justification, and possibly a clearer picture of what to buy.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Utilisation figures can mislead; a fleet at fifty percent average may still be capacity-constrained if the idle half is the wrong hardware for our workloads

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases, while simultaneously preparing a purchase order for two additional GPU nodes that we execute only if utilisation work stalls or demand growth outruns our projections. This is deliberately a sequenced decision rather than a binary one, and the reasoning follows.

**Where we stand**

Our current fleet of eight GPU nodes runs at roughly 34% average utilisation, but that average hides the real problem: utilisation is highly uneven across the day and across workloads. Peak-hour demand on our primary inference cluster saturates capacity, while overnight and weekend utilisation drops into the teens. We are simultaneously capacity-constrained at the moments that matter and wasteful the rest of the time. This pattern is the strongest argument against buying more hardware right now, because a second fleet with the same scheduling behaviour would simply double the waste while doubling the cost.

**Cost**

The capital case for new hardware is easy to state and easy to overstate. Two additional nodes would cost approximately $180,000 up front, plus power, cooling, colocation, and depreciation that push the true annual cost closer to $260,000. Against that, our utilisation work — better batching, request coalescing, a smarter queue, and moving batch-oriented jobs into off-peak windows — requires roughly six engineer-weeks and no capital. If we lift average utilisation from 34% to 55%, which our modelling suggests is achievable, we effectively add the equivalent of one and a half nodes of capacity for a fraction of the purchase price. The economics are not close, provided the utilisation gains actually materialise, which is the main uncertainty in this recommendation.

**Latency**

The risk on the utilisation side is latency. Aggressive batching and queueing improve throughput but can add tens or hundreds of milliseconds to p95 response times, and our product teams have told us that interactive latency is a hard constraint for the customer-facing assistant. This is why the utilisation work must be instrumented against latency SLOs from day one, not treated as a pure throughput exercise. If we find that the batching and scheduling changes that raise utilisation also push p95 latency past our 400ms target, that is a genuine finding, and it changes the calculus: it would mean our remaining headroom is real but unusable for interactive traffic, strengthening the case for purchase. Conversely, if we can shift batch workloads off-peak without touching interactive latency, we buy substantial capacity for free.

**Reliability**

Reliability cuts in favour of buying, and we should be honest about that. Eight nodes is already thin redundancy; a two-node failure during peak currently degrades service noticeably. A larger fleet gives us more failure domains, easier maintenance windows, and less anxiety about correlated load spikes. However, better scheduling also improves reliability in a narrower sense: smoothing demand peaks reduces the queue-depth spikes that cause our occasional timeout cascades. Utilisation work buys us operational stability; hardware buys us fault tolerance. We need both eventually, but the sequencing matters.

**Opportunity cost**

The scarcest resource here is not money but engineer attention. Every week spent on scheduler optimisation is a week not spent on product features. We estimate the utilisation project at six engineer-weeks; if it fails to deliver, we will have spent that time and still face the purchase decision, having lost perhaps six weeks of lead time on hardware that currently ships in ten to fourteen weeks. This is the strongest argument for placing a conditional hardware order now: it converts a future six-week delay into a cancellation fee of zero, since we can defer or cancel before delivery. The option value of that order is high and the cost of holding it is low.

**Reversibility**

Finally, consider reversibility. Hardware purchases are nearly irreversible — once bought, GPUs sit on our balance sheet and shape our architecture for years. Scheduling and batching changes are highly reversible; a bad batching policy can be rolled back in an afternoon. When two options differ this sharply in reversibility, the rational default is to exhaust the reversible option first, keeping the irreversible one in reserve. That is exactly the shape of our recommendation.

**What would change our minds**

If utilisation work shows by mid-quarter that interactive latency binds before 45% utilisation, or if demand forecasts revise upward beyond what even optimistic efficiency gains can absorb, we should execute the hardware order immediately rather than waiting out the quarter. Conversely, if we reach 55% utilisation with latency SLOs intact, we should extend the timeline and revisit in the following quarter.

We'll review progress at the mid-quarter checkpoint and bring data rather than opinions.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Hardware expansion decision for the inference cluster
**Status:** For discussion before Friday's planning session

Over the past few weeks we've been circling a question that deserves a proper answer before we spend anything: should we buy more local AI hardware, or should we invest the same effort in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own? I want to lay out how I see the trade-offs, and then make a recommendation, with the caveat that some of what follows rests on assumptions we should pressure-test together.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward. Our peak demand, particularly during the overnight batch fine-tuning runs and the mid-afternoon spike in interactive inference, occasionally exceeds what the cluster can serve. When that happens, jobs queue, latency degrades from the roughly 200 milliseconds our product team has come to expect to something users notice, and we occasionally fall back to a cloud API at a cost that makes our finance contact wince. Buying more cards would make those peaks painless. It would also give us headroom for the new retrieval-augmented feature planned for next quarter, which we currently have no realistic capacity to serve locally.

But the utilisation numbers complicate that story. Our monitoring suggests the cluster idles at around 35–40% average utilisation across the week. The hardware is heavily loaded for perhaps fifteen hours out of 168; the rest of the time it is mostly warm plastic. That is not an argument that peaks don't matter — they clearly do — but it does suggest the binding constraint is scheduling and workload shaping rather than raw capacity. Several obvious levers exist. Batch inference jobs could be shifted into the overnight window where capacity is abundant. Our model-serving layer currently reserves memory per instance rather than sharing it elastically, which wastes perhaps a fifth of our VRAM. And the queueing behaviour that produces our worst latency spikes is largely an artefact of a first-come-first-served scheduler that treats a background embedding job the same as a user-facing request. A modest investment in a priority queue and better batching would likely eliminate most of the pain we currently attribute to insufficient hardware.

Cost is where the two paths diverge sharply. The expansion option we priced comes in at roughly £90,000 up front, plus ongoing power, cooling, and the less visible cost of someone maintaining it. The utilisation path costs mostly engineering time — call it four to six weeks of one engineer's focus — which is real but is money we are already committed to spending on someone's salary, and the work involved (scheduling, batching, memory management) builds durable competence rather than depreciating. There is also an opportunity cost to consider on both sides: £90,000 spent on silicon is £90,000 not spent on the two product initiatives we keep deferring, and hardware locks us into today's assumptions about model sizes and architectures at a moment when the ground is shifting quickly. Conversely, time spent on utilisation work is time not spent on features, though I'd argue the reliability gains pay that back.

Reliability deserves honest treatment. More hardware does buy genuine redundancy: if a node fails today, we lose a meaningful fraction of capacity, and our single-node failure modes are uglier than I'd like. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, tend to concentrate load and can make the system more fragile if done carelessly — a tightly packed cluster has less slack to absorb a failure. Any utilisation work must therefore preserve headroom deliberately rather than squeezing it away.

On reversibility, the asymmetry is decisive. Hardware is a one-way door: cards depreciate, resale is poor, and unwinding a purchase is slow and loss-making. Scheduling and serving improvements are a revolving door — if they prove insufficient, we can still buy hardware later, having learned exactly how much we actually need. The reverse is not true; buying first teaches us nothing and forecloses nothing except the money.

My recommendation, then: defer the purchase for one quarter. Spend the intervening time on the scheduler, elastic memory allocation, and workload shaping, with a concrete target of raising average utilisation above 60% and cutting p99 latency spikes by half. If we hit those targets and demand still exceeds capacity, we will buy hardware with real evidence in hand — and possibly need less of it. If we miss the targets, we'll have learned something cheaper than a £90,000 lesson.

I'm aware this recommendation carries uncertainty. Utilisation gains are notoriously harder to realise than they look in a planning doc, and if the new RAG feature lands early, we may hit the ceiling before the quarter is out. I propose we set a review checkpoint at week eight with explicit tripwires: if queueing delays breach our latency SLO more than twice in a fortnight, we trigger the purchase
